# Numbers 22 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

4. At the plains of Moab (22:1–36:13)
    * The Balaam story (22:1–24:25)

In this chapter, the king of Moab, Balak, summons a diviner, Balaam, to curse the Israelites. Balaam seems to know Yahweh, the God of Israel. God first prohibits Balaam from going, but eventually allows him to go. However, when Balaam goes, the angel of Yahweh opposes him. Balaam cannot see the angel, but his donkey can, and his donkey eventually speaks to him. After the angel is revealed to Balaam, he warns Balaam to speak only what God wants. Then Balaam meets Balak.

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Cursing

In Balak and Balaam’s culture, people believed that certain people made more effective curses than others. Balaam was a person who could make an effective curse. Balak wants Balaam to say with words bad things that would happen to the Israelites. Then, these bad things would actually happen. People in this culture believed that this kind of curse would work because one of the gods would make the bad things happen. Consider how you might refer to spoken words that cause bad things to happen to people. (See: [curse](tw:curse))

### Balaam’s profession

Numbers 22:7 indicates that Balak’s messengers brought “divinations” with them to Balaam. This indicates that Balaam’s profession was “diviner,” and Joshua 13:22 confirms this by calling Balaam a “diviner.” Divination included several different ways of receiving messages from gods. That included prophecy (speaking directly for a god or gods), receiving and interpreting dreams, and examining events (like the flight of birds) or animal entrails. Balaam encounters God in dreams, speaks for God, and participates in offering sacrifices. All these actions fit with his profession of diviner. Consider how you might refer tot this kind of person in your translation. (See: [divination](tw:divination))

### Why was God angry with Balaam?

God permits Balaam to go with the messengers from Balak. However, once Balaam leaves, God is angry with him for going (22:22). The author does not indicate why God is angry. Some have speculated that Balaam’s intentions are wrong (he only wants money, or he intends to say something contrary to what God wants). Others guess that Balaam is unable to understand what God wants, and so God has to open his eyes. It is recommended that you leave the tension in your translation without explaining it. This best represents what the author of the narrator chose to include.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Introducing Balak

The author first introduces Balak in 22:2. However, the verse does not identify him as a king of Moab. In 22:4, the author again introduces Balak. This time, the verse does identify him as king of Moab. The author probably does this to build suspense. If in your language it would be helpful to introduce more information about Balak earlier, you could include some of the information from verse 4 in verse 2, as the UST does. Alternatively, you could move the information about Balak from verse 4 to verse 2. (See: [Introduction of New and Old Participants](ta:writing-participants))

### Elders of Midian

In 22:4 and 22:7, the author mentions the elders of Midian, who are involved with asking Balaam to curse the Israelites. However, after verse 7, the author never mentions them again. Instead, the focus is on the leaders of Moab. The author may possibly imply that the elders of Midian are still involved. However, it is recommended that you do not include the elders of Midian as implied characters. The author of the passage clearly wanted to focus on the Moabite leaders only from verse 8 onwards.

# Numbers 23 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

4. At the plains of Moab (22:1–36:13)
    * The Balaam story (22:1–24:25)

In this chapter, Balaam pronounces two separate oracles that bless Israel. The first oracle focuses on how God has blessed Israel when Balak wants Balaam to curse Israel. The second oracle focuses on God has acted for the Israelites and how strong the Israelites are.

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Oracles

The word translated “oracle” in verses 7 and 18 is often translated “proverb” or “parable” in other places. Balaam’s speeches are too long to be considered proverbs. In this case, the word “oracle” may indicate that Balaam is speaking in paired lines (see the paragraph on “Parallelism” below) or perhaps that he has put together multiple statements that are like proverbs. Either way, it is clear that Balaam is speaking as a prophet when he delivers these oracles. Consider what word you might use to refer to poetic, prophetic speech.

### Blessing and cursing

See the chapter introduction to Numbers 22 for more information on cursing. People in this culture believed that specific words, spoken by specific people, would have either good or bad effects. The words that led to good effects were blessings, and the words that led to bad effects were curses. In this chapter, Balak asks Balaam to curse the Israelites, but Balaam actually blesses them, as Yahweh commands him to do. (See: [curse](tw:curse) and [bless](tw:bless))

### Different locations

After each of Balaam’s oracles in this chapter, Balak requests that they move to a different location and try again. The author does not state why Balak thinks that a change in location will help Balaam curse the Israelites instead of bless them. He may have thought that a different perspective would change Balaam’s mind. He may have thought that God only had power to control Balaam in certain places. Or he may have thought something else. In your translation, it should be clear that Balaam thinks that a change in location will be helpful, but it is recommended that you do not make explicit why Balak thinks the change in location will help.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Parallelism

Hebrew poetry often expresses ideas through parallelism, where two or more lines say similar things using different words. This repetition creates emphasis and helps the reader understand the meaning more fully. Balaam’s poetic oracles in this and the next chapter use parallelism frequently. When translating parallel lines, you may choose to combine them into a single statement, as the UST often does. Or, you may preserve both lines to reflect the poetic style of the original, connecting them with a word that shows repetition rather than addition. Your translation team should decide how to handle parallelism consistently throughout this chapter. (See: [Parallelism](ta:figs-parallelism))

# Numbers 25 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

4. At the plains of Moab (22:1–36:13)
    * The Israelites are unfaithful to God (25:1–18)

In this chapter, the Israelites worship Baal of Peor with the Moabites, and God punishes them. Then Phinehas kills an Israelite man and a Midianite woman who are involved in the worship, and this atones for the Israelites. God then blesses Phinehas. He also tells the Israelites to attack the Midianites.

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### What were the Israelites doing wrong?

Scholars debate what the Israelites were doing with the Midianite and Moabite women in this chapter. Some think that the Israelites were participating in cultic sexual acts with the women as part of their worship of Baal. Others think that the Israelites were marrying the women and then participating with their wives in the worship of Baal. Either way, it is clear that Israelite men were interacting with the Moabite and Midianite women, and these interactions led to the Israelites worshiping Baal. It is recommended that your translation does not indicate explicitly whether cultic sexual activity or marriage was happening.

### Midianites and Moabites

In [25:1](ta:25), the author indicates that the Moabites are the ones who convinced the Israelites to worship Baal. However, the woman whom Phinehas kills for doing this is a Midianite (see 25:6). Further, when Yahweh tells the Israelites to attack the people who convinced them to worship Baal, he identifies those people as the Midianites. Most likely, this area was populated by both Midianites and Moabites, and both groups of people were probably involved. So, you should leave references to both Moabites and Midianites in this chapter. (See: [midian](tw:midian) and [moab](tw:moab))

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Events narrated out of sequence

When the Israelites worship Baal, God punishes them by sending a plague. However, the author does not mention the plague until the plague is stopped (see 25:8–9). The author implies that the plague was already happening when the Israelites were mourning near the sacred tent (see 25:6). The author may do this to keep the narration concise or to build suspense. Consider how you might indicate that the plague had already started before verses 8–9. (See: [Order of Events](ta:figs-events))

# Numbers 26 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

4. At the plains of Moab (22:1–36:13)
    * A second census (26:1–65)

In this chapter, Moses and Eleazar take a census of the Israelite men who are at least 20 years old and who can be soldiers. They count the Levites separately. This census shows that none of the Israelites who left Egypt are still alive except for Moses, Caleb, and Joshua.

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Census

In this census, Moses and Eleazar list all the Israelite men who are able to fight or, in the case of the Levites, to serve at the sacred tent. They list the men by their clans, which are subgroups within tribes. While the author uses different words in this chapter, the general format is similar to chapter 1. See how you translated the census record there.

### Subclans

For every tribe, the author lists major clans that make up that tribe. In some cases, the author also lists smaller groups within those clans. These smaller groups are sometimes called subclans. Consider what terminology you might use for major groups within a tribe and the smaller groups that make up those major groups. (See: [clan](tw:clan))

### Dividing the land

In 26:53–56, Yahweh gives Moses instructions on how to divide the land up among the tribes. He indicates that larger groups should receive more land than smaller groups. He also indicates that the Israelites should cast lots to see who gets what land. Scholars debate how these two strategies work together. It seems most probable that the Israelites cast lots to see where their land would be, and then they decided on the size of the area based on the size of the tribal group. The author does not directly state whether the lots were cast for each tribe, for each clan, or for each individual. Because the census earlier in the chapter focuses on individual clans, the UST indicates that these instructions are about clans.

### Lots

In 26:53–56, Yahweh gives Moses instructions on how to divide up the land among the Israelites. These instructions include using lots. Using lots was a way to randomize decisions. Lots could be cast, which would mean rolling or throwing marked stones or pieces of wood to see which side would land upright. Lots could be drawn, which would mean picking marked items without looking at the marks. In this culture, people believed that the decisions, although random from a human perspective, were directed by God. Consider how you might refer to this way of making decisions, which removes human choice but leaves open divine choice. (See: [lots](tw:lots))

### The Levites

In 26:57–62. Moses and Eleazar count the Levites. The author states why the Levites are counted separately. They do not receive land, so they are not counted among the rest of the Israelites in this census. Additionally, every male who is at least one month old is counted, unlike with the rest of the Israelites, who are counted if they are at least 20 years old. The placement of the Levites after the list of the rest of the Israelites shows that the Levites are set apart for God.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Repetition and variation

Many of the entries in this list use the exact same wording. However, in some cases the wording is slightly different, with some words omitted or other words chosen instead. See the ULT for a representation of the differences. Unless the differences are significant, the UST generally models how to keep the entries similar.

### Large numbers

The numbers in this chapter are all over 10,000. Consider how you would express large numbers in your language and use that form consistently in this chapter. See how you translated the large numbers in [chapter 1](ta:01).

### Breaks in the list

In 26:8–11 and 26:19, the author interrupts the census list to give some details about specific people or groups within a tribe. Consider how you might introduce and format these breaks in the list.

4. At the plains of Moab (22:1–36:13)
    * The daughters of Zelophehad (27:1–11)
    * Moses commissions Joshua (27:12–23)

In the first half of this chapter, the daughters of Zelophehad request land in the name of their father, although he had no sons. Yahweh grants their request and provides instructions regarding inheritance. In the second half of this chapter, Yahweh tells Moses that he will die before entering the land. He also tells Moses to commission Moses to be the next leader of the Israelites, along with Eleazar the priest.

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Children and inheritance

In this culture, when a father died, his sons usually inherited his land and property. This practice maintained land and property within one group that was descended from a single ancestor. In this chapter, the daughters of a man who had no sons make a request. They want to inherit their father’s land and property. That way, a portion of their tribe’s land will continue to belong to the descendants of their father, just like it will for their father’s brothers. Yahweh agrees that this is the right thing to do. Daughters should inherit their father’s land and property if there are no sons. Only if there are also no daughters should the land and property be inherited by other relatives, like brothers or uncles.

### Commissioning Joshua

When Moses learns that he will soon die, he asks Yahweh to appoint a leader who will replace him. Yahweh tells Moses to commission Joshua. Joshua will only share some of Moses’ glory, and he will have to communicate with God through the high priest instead of directly. However, he will be the next leader of the Israelites. Moses signifies this by laying his hands on Joshua.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### When does the story in 27:12–23 happen?

The Hebrew conjunction that begins the story in 27:12 does not indicate that the events narrated in this story happened immediately after the events in the story in [27:1–11](ta:27). These events may have happened before or after daughters of Zelophehad asked to inherit their father’s land. Consider how you might introduce the story in 27:12–23 in a way that does not indicate that the events narrated in it immediately follow the events narrated in the previous story. (See: [Order of Events](ta:figs-events))

## Structure and Formatting

4. At the plains of Moab (22:1–36:13)
    * Instructions for regular and festival offerings (28:1–29:40)

In this chapter, Yahweh gives instructions concerning the animals, grain, and wine that the Israelites needed to offer to him on certain days. That includes offerings for every day, for Sabbath days, for the first days of months, for the Festival of Unleavened Bread, and for the day of firstfruits during the Festival of Weeks.

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Grain and drink offerings

This chapter includes instructions for what the Israelites were supposed to offer along with animal sacrifices. For each male lamb, ram, and bull that they offered, they needed to offer also a specific portion of grain and wine. The portion size was different for each animal. When the Israelites included the grain and drink offerings with each animal, Yahweh was pleased. (See: [mealoffering](tw:mealoffering) and [drinkoffering](tw:drinkoffering))

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Quotes in quotes

Most of this chapter is part of a long quote within another quote. The ULT represents the quote within a quote. The UST models how to express the idea with only one level of quotation. Consider how your language indicates that a quote contains a quote. (See: [Quotes within Quotes](ta:figs-quotesinquotes))

### “a scent of pleasing”

Multiple times in this chapter, Yahweh describes a sacrifice as “a scent of pleasing” to or for him. This phrase refers to burning the sacrifice in a way that causes smoke to go up, picturing the sacrifice as being converted to pleasant-smelling smoke by the fire and arising to Yahweh in heaven, where he would smell the smoke and be pleased. That the sacrifice was accompanied by the gift of the pleasant-smelling smoke of the sacrifice was apparently crucial to the acceptance of the offering as an appropriate sacrifice on a person’s behalf.

### Second person singular and plural

Throughout this chapter, most occurrences of “you” are plural. There are a few exceptions. In 28:2–3, when Yahweh is commanding Moses what to say, “you” is singular. Further, in 28:4, 8, and 21, “you” is singular. It is possible that “you” in these verses refers to the individual person who was offering the animals. (See: [Forms of ‘You’ — Singular](ta:figs-yousingular))

### Omitted words in the lists of offerings

Throughout this chapter, the instructions for grain offerings are given in abbreviated form. Two kinds of words are left out.

First, the verb is often omitted. Where the ULT reads simply “and two tenths of fine flour,” the reader is expected to supply “you shall offer” from the earlier instructions. If your language requires a verb in such statements, you may need to include one. (See: [Ellipsis](ta:figs-ellipsis))

Second, the unit of measure is omitted. “A tenth” and “two tenths” mean a tenth part and two tenth parts of an ephah, a standard dry measure. If your readers would be confused by a fraction with nothing to divide, you could supply the unit and translate this as “a tenth of an ephah.” (See: [translate-fractions](ta:translate-fractions))

# Numbers 30 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

4. At the plains of Moab (22:1–36:13)
    * Vows and agreements by women (30:1–15)

In this chapter, Moses recounts instructions concerning vows and agreements made by women. The instructions deal with four situations: an unmarried woman living with her parents, a woman who has recently gotten married, a divorced woman or widow, and a woman who is married. In each case, if the woman is part of a man’s household, the man is responsible for confirming or nullifying the woman’s vow or agreement.

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Household structure and authority

In this culture, the person who had authority over the whole household was the oldest male. So, a daughter living at home with her parents or a married woman living with her husband was under the authority of the man, whether her father or her husband. However, for a widow or divorced woman, there was no man with authority over her. Given this way of structuring households, this chapter indicates that the person in charge of the household (usually the husband or father) was responsible for confirming or nullifying any promises or agreements made by the women in the household.

### Vows

Vows were promises that a person made to God. Often, the person would ask God to do something and then promise to do something or give something to God if God did what the person asked. Consider how you might refer to this kind of solemn promise made to God. (See: [oath](tw:oath))

### Oaths

Oaths were statements that confirmed promises and commitments. Oaths could call God as witness, or they could specify the consequences if the promise or commitment was broken. Consider how you might refer to this kind of solemn confirming statement. (See: [oath](tw:oath))

### Bonds

The word translated as “bond” in this chapter occurs only here in the Hebrew Bible. Scholars debate exactly what it means. It could refer to a promise not to do something, while “vow” refers to a promise to do something. More likely, it refers to a binding agreement, sometimes written, with a person or people. The UST follows that interpretation. Consider how you might refer to a binding agreement between people.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### What is the class of the woman in 30:10–15?

Some scholars argue that 30:10–15 or 30:10–12 continues to speak about the same woman as 30:9 does: a divorced or widowed woman. In this case, 30:10–15 or 30:10–12 refer to the time before the woman was widowed or divorced. Other scholars argue that 3:10–15 deal with a new situation: a woman who is married when she makes vows or agreements. This seems to make more sense of the present tense verbs in 30:12. The UST follows this interpretation.

# Numbers 31 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

4. At the plains of Moab (22:1–36:13)
    * Battle with Midian, cleansing, and plunder (31:1–54)

In this chapter, the Israelites attack and defeat the Midianites (31:1–12). When the soldiers return, Moses and Eleazar give them commands about how they and their plunder should be purified (31:13–24). After that, Yahweh gives Moses instructions about how to divide the plunder among the soldiers, the rest of the Israelites, the priests, and the Levites, which Moses follows (31:25–47). Finally, the commanders of the army offer a special gift to Yahweh because none of the Israelite soldiers died (31:48–54).

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### War for Yahweh

When the Israelites fought wars that Yahweh commanded them to fight, they sometimes killed all the men of the people they were fighting. That is what they do when they defeat the Midianites in this chapter. While God does not give explicit instructions, Moses also requires the Israelites to kill the boys and the women who have had sex. These actions are very violent, and scholars interpret the meaning in different ways. It is recommended that translations simply represent the violence.

### Purity and impurity

This chapter refers back to concepts that were important in Numbers 19. Those concepts include impurity because of dead bodies and the special water that the Israelites could use to cleanse this impurity. In this chapter, the soldiers, captives, and plunder are impure. The people must be cleansed by washing with the special water as they wait outside the camp for seven days. The plunder must be cleansed by the special water and, in some cases, by fire. Once everything is cleansed, the people and plunder may enter the Israelite camp. (See: [purify](tw:purify) and [defile](tw:defile))

### The levy for Yahweh and the Levites

This chapter refers to a “levy” from the plunder that the Israelites needed to pay to Yahweh and to the Levites. Moses first divided the plunder in half. One half was for the soldiers who had fought in the battle. From this half, they had to give one out of every 500 people and animals to Yahweh as the “levy.” Yahweh then granted this levy to Eleazar and the rest of the priests. From the other half that belonged to the rest of the Israelites, they had to give one out of every 50 people and animals to the Levites. Some translations refer to this “levy” as a tax or a tribute. Consider how you might refer to the levy in your language.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Balaam

This chapter refers to the same Balaam from Numbers 22–24. The Israelites killed him when they attacked the Midianites (see 31:8). Later in the chapter (31:16), Moses indicates that Balaam was the one who told the Midianites to convince the Israelites to worship Baal of Peor, which is narrated in Numbers 25. Consider how you can make it clear to your readers that this chapter refers to the same Balaam from Numbers 22–24 and the same event from Numbers 25.

### Hyperbole

In this chapter, the narrator speaks as if the Israelites had completely destroyed all the Midianite men and cities and had taken every single thing that the Midianites owned. However, it is clear from later stories that many Midianites were not killed (for example, see the story in Judges 6. The narrator may be using hyperbole to indicate that the Israelites defeated and killed many Midianites. Or, the narrator may mean that the Israelites defeated and killed all the men in a specific group of Midianites. It is recommended that you preserve the strong language in your translation, but you could include a footnote explaining what the extreme language may mean.

### Large numbers

There are many large numbers in this chapter, including many over 10,000. Consider how you would express large numbers in your language and use that form consistently in this chapter. See how you translated the large numbers in chapter 1.

# Numbers 32 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

4. At the plains of Moab (22:1–36:13)
    * People from Gad, Reuben, and Manasseh choose to settle on the east side of the Jordan River (32:1–42)

In this chapter, Moses, Joshua, Eleazar, and the Israelite leaders make an agreement with the leaders of the tribes of Gad and Reuben. This agreement specifies that the soldiers from Gad and Reuben must help the rest of the Israelites conquer the land west of the Jordan River. However, once that is done, the people of Gad and Reuben receive land on the east side of the Jordan River. The chapter also briefly recounts some people from Manasseh who also conquered and received land on the east side of the Jordan River.

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Land on the east side and west side of the Jordan River

The land of Canaan itself was on the west side of the Jordan River. However, the Israelites conquered some land on the east side of the Jordan River. People from Gad, Reuben, and part of the tribe of Manasseh wanted to receive this land on the east side of the Jordan. Moses initially rejects their desire, but eventually he allows them to receive this land as long as they help the rest of the Israelites conquer the land of Canaan on the west side of the Jordan River.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### What did the Reubenites and Gadites request?

When the people from the tribes of Reuben and Gad request land on the east side of the Jordan River, they do not specify exactly what they mean. They may mean that they will settle in that land and refuse to help the rest of the Israelites conquer Canaan. This is what Moses thinks they mean. They may mean that they will settle in that land but will still help the rest of the Israelites conquer Canaan. This is what they offer in response to Moses’ rejection of their initial request. If possible, you should preserve this ambiguity in your translation of their initial request.

### Quotes in quotes

In 32:11–12, there is a quote inside a quote. Consider how your language indicates that a quote contains a quote. The UST models how to express the idea with only one level of quotations. (See: [Quotes within Quotes](ta:figs-quotesinquotes))

### Timing of events

The events that the author narrates in 32:39–42 almost certainly did not happen after the events narrated earlier in the chapter. They probably happened sometime around the events narrated in Numbers 21. Additionally, each specific battle that the author narrates may have happened at the same time or in a different sequence. Consider how you can introduce these events so that it is clear they do not follow the previous events in chronological sequence. (See: [Order of Events](ta:figs-events))

# Numbers 33 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

4. At the plains of Moab (22:1–36:13)
    * Itinerary from Egypt to the plains of Moab (33:1–49)
    * Instructions on possessing the land (33:50–56)

In this chapter, the narrator records places where the Israelites camped on the way from Egypt to the plains of Moab. At the end of the chapter, Yahweh gives Moses instructions on how the Israelites should conquer and divide the land.

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Dividing the land

In 33:54, Yahweh gives Moses instructions on how to divide the land up among the tribes. He indicates that larger groups should receive more land than smaller groups. He also indicates that the Israelites should cast lots to see who gets what land. Scholars debate how these two strategies work together. It seems most probable that the Israelites cast lots to see where their land would be, and then they decided on the size of the area based on the size of the tribal group. See how you translated the similar instructions in 26:53–56.

### Lots

In 33:54, Yahweh gives Moses instructions on how to divide up the land among the Israelites. These instructions include using lots. Using lots was a way to randomize decisions. Lots could be cast, which would mean rolling or throwing marked stones or pieces of wood to see which side would land upright. Lots could be drawn, which would mean picking marked items without looking at the marks. In this culture, people believed that the decisions, although random from a human perspective, were directed by God. Consider how you might refer to this way of making decisions, which removes human choice but leaves open divine choice. See how you translated the instructions concerning lots in 26:53–56. (See: [lots](tw:lots))

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Unknown locations

Many of the places named in this chapter are unknown to contemporary scholars. Not only is it uncertain where the places were, but it is also uncertain what kind of places they were. Each of the place names could be a town, a wadi, a hill, an oasis, or something else. Because of this uncertainty, it is recommended that you refer to these places as generically as you can.

# Numbers 34 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

4. At the plains of Moab (22:1–36:13)
    * The borders of Canaan (34:1–15)
    * The leaders for inheriting the land (34:16–29)

In this chapter, Yahweh tells Moses what the borders of Canaan, the land the Israelites must conquer and live in, should be. Moses explains this to the Israelites, along with a reminder about the two and one half tribes on the east side of the Jordan River. Then, Yahweh appoints twelve men to oversee the process of deciding which tribes and clans receive which parts of Canaan.

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### The borders of Canaan

In the first part of this chapter, Yahweh outlines the borders of Canaan. He describes a shape that is almost a rectangle. He starts at the southeast corner, which is the bottom of the Sea of Salt. The south side is a curved line from there to the Mediterranean Sea. The west side simply follows the Mediterranean Sea. The north side begins in the west at the Mediterranean Sea and goes east, somewhere above the Sea of Chinnereth. The east side begins somewhere above the Sea of Chinnereth and goes south to the southern part of the Sea of Salt. While the Israelites did not succeed in conquering all this territory, this is the area that Yahweh instructed them to conquer.

### Inheriting the land

In the second half of this chapter, Yahweh speaks of leaders “inheriting the land.” This phrase refers to the process of dividing the land up into sections. The leaders would then assign each section to a tribal group or family. They would do this using lots (see the chapter introduction to Numbers 33 for more information on lots). Yahweh ensures that at least one leader from each tribe was involved in this process.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Unknown locations

Much like in chapter 33, many of the place names in the first half of this chapter are unknown. Not only is it uncertain where the places were, it is also uncertain what kind of places they were. Each of the place names could be a town, a wadi, a hill, an oasis, or something else. Because of this uncertainty, it is recommended that you refer to most of these places as generically as you can.

# Numbers 35 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

4. At the plains of Moab (22:1–36:13)
    * Cities for the Levites (35:1–8)
    * Instructions concerning intentional and unintentional killing (35:9–34)

In this chapter, Yahweh gives Moses instructions. The first part of the instructions indicates the number and size of cities and pasturelands that the Levites were to receive from the rest of the Israelites. The second part of the instructions indicates how the Israelites should deal with intentional and unintentional killings.

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Cities of refuge

Six of the cities that the Israelites were supposed to give to the Levites functioned as cities of refuge. When a person killed someone, he or she normally deserved to be killed by the dead person’s close relative. However, if the person killed someone by accident, the person could flee to one of the six cities. If he or she stayed in that city, the dead person’s close relative was not allowed to kill him or her. In this way, the city provided refuge, or safety, for someone who unintentionally killed someone else. Eventually, that person would stand trial to confirm whether they killed someone unintentionally or intentionally.

### One redeeming the blood

This chapter describes a close relative of a person who was killed as “one redeeming the blood.” This phrase fits with what Yahweh says in 35:33–34. When a person kills someone (sheds their blood), redemption or atonement needs to be accomplished. The close relative could accomplish this redemption by killing the murderer. In this way, they “redeemed the blood” of their relative and made things right before God. (See: [bloodshed](tw:bloodshed) and [redeem](tw:redeem))

### Intentional and unintentional killing

This chapter distinguishes carefully between intentional killing (murder) and unintentional killing (manslaughter). The criteria for deciding between murder and manslaughter include the weapon used, the way the person died, the relationship between the people, and whether the action was intentional or accidental. Consider what words you might use to distinguish between murder (intentional killing) and manslaughter (unintentional killing).

### The death of the high priest

Yahweh indicates that a person who killed someone unintentionally would have to stay in a city of refuge until the high priest died. What the high priest’s death accomplishes is not directly stated. Most likely, the high priest’s death atoned for all the unintentional killings during his time as high priest. This is like the sacrifices offered on the Day of the Atonement, which atoned for many sins committed throughout the year. However, since Yahweh does not make the function of the high priest’s death explicit, it is recommended that you also do not make it explicit in your translation.

### Polluting the land

In 35:33–34, Yahweh explains that whenever someone is killed, it pollutes or defiles the land where the Israelites live. This is not good, since Yahweh was present with the Israelites in the land. Because Yahweh was present, both the Israelites and their land needed to be pure. So, it was very important for the Israelites to deal with murder and manslaughter properly. Only executing a murderer and keeping a manslayer in a city of refuge would keep the land pure. These verses provide the motivation for following the commands earlier in the chapter. (See: [purify](tw:purify) and [defile](tw:defile))

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Metonymy with blood

Yahweh refers to “blood” ten times in this chapter. Blood can refer to death, or even more specifically to murder. It can also refer to the guilt from killing someone. See the UST for the meaning in each case. Blood is an important figure of speech in the Bible, so if possible include references to blood in your translation. (See: [bloodshed](tw:bloodshed) and [Metonymy](ta:figs-metonymy))

### Singular and plural “you”

Most instances of “you” in this chapter are plural. The only exceptions are when Yahweh is speaking directly to Moses in 35:2 and 35:10 and when Yahweh addresses each individual Israelite at the beginning of 35:34. (See: [Forms of ‘You’ — Singular](ta:figs-yousingular))

# Numbers 36 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

4. At the plains of Moab (22:1–36:13)
    * Instructions concerning daughters who inherit land (36:1–12)
    * Conclusion for instructions at the plains of Moab (36:13)

In this chapter, Moses gives Yahweh’s instructions concerning keeping ancestral land within a tribe when daughters inherit that land. He gives specific instructions for Zelophehad’s daughters, which continue from [27:1–11](ta:27), and then more general instructions. Daughters that inherit land must marry someone from the same tribe to keep ancestral land within that tribe. The chapter ends with a brief conclusion to this section of Numbers.

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Property, marriage, and inheritance

In this culture, when a woman married a man, the man would be in charge of any property or possessions that the woman had. If the woman had inherited land from her father, that land would now belong to her husband. If the husband was from a different tribe than the wife, the land would permanently belong to a different tribe than the tribe of the wife’s father. This situation is what the leaders of Manasseh wish to avoid. Yahweh tells Moses to agree with them and require women who have inherited land to marry within their tribe. That way, the property would continue to belong to their father’s tribe. (See: [inherit](tw:inherit) and [marriage](tw:marriage))

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Marriage within the tribe or the clan?

In 36:6 and 36:8, Moses indicates whom daughters who inherit may marry. It is possible that he means that they must marry someone from the same tribe and clan as their father. It is possible that he means only that they must marry someone from the same tribe as their father. The UST follows that interpretation. See the notes on these verses for alternate translations.
